newsitem.title: USA: Senate to vote in week on Pena as energy secretary.
newsitem.headline: Senate to vote in week on Pena as energy secretary.

text.p: A Republican U.S. senator on Thursday said he would delay a full Senate vote to confirm Energy Secretary nominee Federico Pena until he receives a White House plan on how it will dispose of radioactive waste from nuclear power plants.

"I believe that the Senate must not rush ahead in confirming Mr. Pena's nomination before we receive from him a specific and constructive response to our questions," Rod Grams, of Minnesota, said on the Senate floor.

"Accordingly, I would object to any unanimous consent agreement to bring up Mr. Pena's nomination for a vote at this time," Grams said. Under Senate rules, a single lawmaker can bring movement on an issue to a virtual halt.
A White House spokesman said he expected the vote would be held soon, despite the Grams statement. "We're confident it will be worked out by early next week," he said.
Earlier Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi said he would have liked to have taken up Pena's confirmation on) Thursday, but expected it would be done within a week.

Pena's bid to replace former Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary has been dogged by a number of Republicans' complaints that the White House has shirked its responsibilty to find a way to store the waste from nuclear power plants.

Under a 1982 law, the federal government is to take responsibility for the nuclear waste next January. Utilities have paid some $12 billion into a federal fund to build a central site for the waste, but it is still in planning stages.

The Senate Energy Committee earlier on Thursday voted 19-0 to forward Pena's nomination to the full Senate. The vote came after several weeks of delay imposed by Committee Chairman Frank Murkowski, an Alaska Republican who also said the administration must come to grips with the nuclear waste issue.
"The main issue is and has been whether the new secretary will have authority to work with Congress on the nuclear waste problem," Murkowski said before the vote.
After meetings last week with White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles, Murkowski said he felt the administration was more willing to discuss the issue, and he cleared Pena's vote.
But Grams, who declined to vote in favour of Pena and only voted "present," said the administration's response so far has been unsatisfactory.

The administration is evaluating whether to put a permanent dump at Nevada's Yucca Mountain, but it would be 15 or more years before that site is ready to accept the waste now scattered at some 80 locations across the country.
Running out of storage space and facing local oppostion, utilities are suing the federal government to take the waste on time, which could require a temporary storage measure.
